title: Marilyn Diptych
lede: Andy Warhol’s fifty repeated Marilyn Monroe heads on two canvases: a grid in flat color on the left, fading black and white on the right.
summary: Fifty silkscreened faces in a grid, colored on one panel and black on the other. Andy Warhol, 1962.

evidence.note: Tate serves images of this work only up to 256 px wide; larger sizes return HTTP 403. The 256 px image confirms only the two-panel grid, which is too small for observation. Description relies on Tate’s record and Wikipedia.

styles.note: The key source for the style’s grid of repeated units and for the Warhol color variant. Partial fit: it has no dots, key lines, or comic devices.

context: Tate gives the medium as alkyd ink, acrylic paint, oil ground, and graphite on two canvases. [Tate](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/warhol-marilyn-diptych-t03093).

Warhol made the work in 1962, shortly after Monroe’s death in August. It repeats fifty images from a publicity still for the 1953 film *Niagara* by Gene Kornman: colored portraits on the left panel and fading black-and-white impressions on the right. Tate acquired it in 1980. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Diptych).

Warhol described silkscreening as picking a photograph, blowing it up, transferring it in glue onto silk, and rolling ink across it, so that each image is the same but slightly different. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Diptych).
A later screenprint of the same head is [Marilyn Monroe (Marilyn)](ref:warhol-marilyn-screenprint-1967).
interpretation: The diptych gives the style its second layout: not one enlarged panel but a strict grid of identical units, like goods on a shelf or frames on a contact sheet.
The contrast between the two panels depends on print variation. On screen, the equivalent is a grid in which units vary slightly in ink density or registration.
borrow: Repeat one image in a tight grid with no gutters, and vary only its color or density from cell to cell.
Pair a colored grid with a monochrome grid of the same unit.
next: Inspect an image at least 800 px wide and add observed traits.
